### Observed differences

- On six activities — A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 — work shifted from one group of resources to a largely different group. In the earlier window the leading performers included User_42 at roughly 7–8 in 100 executions of each activity (the earlier leader on A22 held about 10 in 100); in the later window those resources had fallen to about 4–5 in 100 or dropped out of the leading group altogether (A01), while a largely different group including User_56 rose from unlisted or about 3 in 100 to about 6–8 in 100, and to about 14 in 100 on A22. The direction of shift is the same on all six activities, and it is largest for A22 (dissimilarity about 0.57 versus about 0.26–0.29 for the others). Each profile rests on roughly 95–250 observations per window. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007]
- A16 moved from being shared across about eleven resources (largest shares about 16 in 100 each) to being performed entirely by a single resource, User_28: the concentration index rose from about 0.11 to 1.0 and the number of distinct resources fell from 15 to 1, on similar volumes (about 145 versus 137 executions). [ASSIGN005, CONC001]
- No control-flow or timing difference passed the screening thresholds (0 qualifying items in each of those families, against roughly 0.2 and 0.01 expected by chance), so the qualifying differences are confined to how work was allocated to resources. [screening]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports a change in resource allocation: on A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22, execution was reassigned from one group of resources to another. In the earlier window these activities were led by resources such as User_42 (about 7–8 in 100 executions each); in the later window a largely different group including User_56 holds the largest shares on all of them, with the same direction of shift on every activity. No structural or timing difference qualified, so the change is specific to allocation rather than accompanied by added, removed or reordered activities. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, screening]

The support is direct and consistent: the ASSIGN indicator measures which resource performed each activity, the same gaining and losing groups recur across all six activities, the resource family produced 8 qualifying items where about 0.005 would be expected if nothing had changed — a count chance cannot plausibly produce — and every item's difference is larger than in all but about 1 of 2000 random re-splits of the pooled data. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN006, ASSIGN007, CONC001, screening]

Limitations: the evidence cannot distinguish a reassignment of work from a change in which resources were active in each window or in the mix of cases handled, since it contains no case-attribute or handover information and the resource codes are anonymous. A13 and A14 show identical profiles and may reflect a single underlying behaviour rather than two. [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004]

Other differences: A16 shows a distinct allocation change — from about eleven resources sharing the work to one resource, User_28, performing all of it (concentration index about 0.11 to 1.0) — a move to full concentration rather than a redistribution between groups. [ASSIGN005, CONC001]
